content: Data were collected from community members and elders in Zimbabwe through 85 interviews and eight focus group discussions, both before the introduction of point-of-care (POC) testing and after it had been in use for at least three months. The reduced time to receive test results significantly alleviated caregiver anxiety regarding the child’s HIV status and enabled families to initiate treatment earlier. Some individuals perceived printed POC results as more reliable than handwritten results, believing that this reduced the likelihood of human error. However, a few expressed distrust in HIV results that were generated too quickly. Caregivers generally supported POC infant testing, but further collaboration with community groups is necessary to enhance acceptance and demand. Among people living with HIV, 72% found it acceptable to collect samples, conduct testing, and provide results within one hour. Additionally, 51% of respondents believed that knowing the HIV status as soon as possible was worthwhile, and 41% recognized the benefit of same-day testing and results in enabling immediate treatment initiation. A majority (81%) found same-day testing, diagnosis, and treatment initiation for infants acceptable. Furthermore, 74% of people living with HIV believed that nurses could test infants for HIV and provide results during the same visit, and 72% expressed confidence in healthcare workers’ ability to perform these tasks. A study conducted across eight African countries (Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Zimbabwe) involved structured interviews with healthcare workers providing infant testing services and semi-structured interviews with national and regional laboratory managers or early infant diagnosis program managers, both before and after POC infant testing implementation. Healthcare workers found POC infant testing easy to use, with 74% describing it as very simple to perform. They were highly satisfied with the rapid turnaround time and the ability to initiate treatment for HIV-positive infants sooner, with 93% expressing satisfaction. All healthcare workers recommended scaling up POC infant testing in their countries, and 87% desired a POC testing device in their healthcare facilities. Laboratory managers also supported scaling up POC testing but emphasized the need for reliable infrastructure to operate the platforms. An online survey of 51 healthcare workers and 53 program managers assessed the acceptability and feasibility of implementing POC infant testing. Among healthcare workers, 88% felt comfortable running the test, delivering results, counseling, and initiating treatment on the same day. Most healthcare workers (77%) found POC infant testing acceptable, and 65% preferred it if available. Additionally, 88% believed that mothers would accept same-day infant testing and, in some cases, positive diagnoses. However, 45% of healthcare workers anticipated an increased workload in clinics due to POC testing, though they believed sufficient human resources were available for implementation. Among program managers, 72% reported that their countries already had policies for POC infant testing, but 85% indicated that most infant tests were still conducted using standard laboratory-based methods. A majority (55%) considered POC infant testing preferable and feasible, and more than half (55%) did not believe that implementing POC testing would increase the workload in laboratories or clinics. A systematic review of diagnostic accuracy for POC technologies revealed high performance, with sensitivity exceeding 98% and specificity greater than 99%. Two POC devices, Abbott m-PIMA™ and Cepheid GeneXpert®, have WHO prequalification and are already in use for tuberculosis and infant HIV diagnosis. These devices use whole blood and do not require additional equipment or expertise. The Abbott m-PIMA™ device can perform 6–8 tests per day, while the Cepheid GeneXpert® can process 6–8 tests per module daily. Across 140 high-burden developing countries, over 11,600 devices comprising 52,000 modules have been delivered, leaving capacity for expanding TB testing and considering HIV infant testing. Infant diagnosis should remain a priority when technologies are shared across programs. Ethical and equity considerations emphasized the fair distribution of benefits and burdens at the population level, ensuring that infants are not disadvantaged relative to others in their communities. If the introduction of POC testing does not harm the broader community by diverting resources, there is no clear argument against its implementation. The Guideline Development Group strongly recommended POC nucleic acid testing for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months of age. This recommendation was based on the overwhelming benefits of the intervention, including faster testing and result delivery, increased retention in the testing-to-treatment cascade, fewer healthcare visits for caregivers, improved reliability and documentation of results, increased equity with adult HIV testing, faster access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), reduced mortality, and improved service quality. No major harms were identified, though higher costs of testing, the need for extensive network support, and greater technical support and maintenance requirements were noted. Implementation considerations included integrating POC technologies into existing infant diagnosis algorithms, expanding access to high-quality diagnostic testing, and optimizing the placement of POC technologies within the health system. Adequate human resources, training, and quality assurance must be ensured, along with clear communication and collaboration with community groups to support demand generation and utilization. Research gaps include the need for further implementation research on quality assurance approaches to sustain POC testing delivery for infant diagnosis. Investigating dual-claim POC tests for use across infants, children, and adults for both HIV diagnosis and viral load monitoring could streamline supply chains and improve diagnostic systems. Device-free tests closer to traditional rapid diagnostic tests are also being developed, which could support decentralization and require no capital investment for low-volume healthcare facilities. Diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact studies for these tests would be beneficial. For viral load testing, POC technologies may be used to monitor treatment among people living with HIV receiving ART. These technologies simplify testing, require minimal expertise, and return results within 1–2 hours. Two such technologies have undergone WHO prequalification and are now available for procurement. POC viral load testing is particularly beneficial for populations requiring rapid results, such as those with advanced HIV disease, infants, children, adolescents, individuals with suspected treatment failure, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. A systematic review comparing POC viral load testing with laboratory-based methods identified moderate to high-certainty evidence. POC testing significantly reduced the time to return results to clinicians and patients compared to standard methods. In a randomized controlled trial, 99% of patients received same-day results with POC testing, compared to only 82% with standard testing. Long-term outcomes showed that 90% of patients who received POC testing achieved viral suppression and retention in care after 12 months, compared to 76% with standard testing.
